name: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
description: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 is the authoritative catalog of security and privacy controls for federal information systems and organizations, used with FIPS 199 categorization and the Risk Management Framework to select baselines, tailor controls, and achieve authorization. An audit of an 800-53 environment tests whether the system is correctly categorized, the baseline is properly selected and tailored, controls are implemented as documented in the System Security Plan, and continuous monitoring keeps the authorization current. Auditors should expect to trace findings into a living POA&M process.
tagline: The U.S. federal catalog of security and privacy controls used to select, implement, assess, and continuously monitor protections for information systems.
auditFocus: Correct FIPS 199 security categorization and selection of the low, moderate, or high control baseline
Quality and accuracy of the System Security Plan (SSP) as the authoritative description of control implementation
Operating effectiveness of management, operational, and technical controls across all 20 families
Continuous monitoring strategy (CA-7) and whether assessment results actually drive control updates
POA&M discipline: finding documentation, remediation milestones, risk acceptance, and closure evidence
Supply chain risk management controls (SR family), new in Revision 5

phases.name: Phase 1 — Planning, System Categorization & Baseline Selection
phases.objective: Establish what system is being audited, confirm it is correctly categorized under FIPS 199, verify the right 800-53 baseline was selected and tailored, and confirm the SSP and authorization approach exist before testing begins.

questions.question: Walk me through how this system was categorized under FIPS 199. What information types did you identify, and what confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact levels were assigned to each?
questions.whyItMatters: The security categorization drives the entire control baseline. If the system is under-categorized, the organization is protecting it with too few controls; if over-categorized, money is wasted on controls that don't fit the risk.
questions.guidance: A good answer names specific information types (e.g., from NIST SP 800-60), assigns explicit low/moderate/high impact levels for each security objective, shows the system-level categorization as the high-water mark, and has System Owner and Authorizing Official sign-off.
probes: When was the categorization last reviewed, and what triggered the review?
Did any information type drive the system to moderate or high impact? Which one?

questions.question: Which control baseline was selected for this system (low, moderate, or high), and how does that map back to the FIPS 199 categorization?
questions.whyItMatters: Baseline selection translates the categorization into the actual set of controls the system must implement. A mismatch between impact level and baseline is a foundational audit finding.
questions.guidance: The baseline must match the highest impact level across the three security objectives (high-water mark). The interviewee should produce the list of controls in the selected baseline and show it is the Rev. 5 baseline, not a legacy Rev. 4 set.
probes: Is this system subject to any overlays (e.g., privacy, CUI) that added controls beyond the base baseline?
How many controls are in your tailored baseline?

questions.question: How was the baseline tailored? Which controls were scoped out, added, or had parameters adjusted, and where is each tailoring decision documented and justified?
questions.whyItMatters: Tailoring is legitimate only when decisions are documented, risk-based, and approved. Undocumented 'we don't do that control' answers usually hide unmitigated risk or an inaccurate SSP.
evidence: Risk-based justification memos for removed controls
questions.guidance: Expect a documented tailoring record: organization-defined parameters filled in (e.g., time periods, lists of personnel), compensating control rationale for anything scoped out, and evidence the Authorizing Official accepted the tailored baseline.
probes: Show me one control you tailored out and the justification.
Who approved the tailored baseline, and when?

questions.controlRef: PL-2 System Security and Privacy Plan
questions.question: Show me the System Security Plan. How current is it, and does it accurately describe the system boundary, the environment of operation, and how each control in the tailored baseline is implemented?
questions.whyItMatters: The SSP is the single source of truth an auditor tests against. An SSP that doesn't match reality means either the controls aren't implemented as claimed or the documentation process is broken — both are findings.
evidence: SSP revision history and review records
questions.guidance: A strong answer includes a recently reviewed SSP (within the last year or after major change), a clear boundary description separating the system from interconnections, and per-control implementation narratives written in the system's own terms — not boilerplate copied from 800-53.
probes: Pick one control narrative — walk me to where that actually happens in the environment.
What is the process for updating the SSP when the system changes?

questions.question: What is the current authorization status of this system? Who is the Authorizing Official, when was the ATO (or denial/interim authorization) issued, and on what evidence was it based?
questions.whyItMatters: Operating without a current authorization, or holding an ATO based on stale assessments, means senior leadership may be accepting risk they have never actually seen.
evidence: Security assessment report supporting the ATO
questions.guidance: Expect a named Authorizing Official, an ATO with a defined expiration or ongoing-authorization status, and an authorization package consisting of the SSP, a recent security assessment report, and a POA&M. 'We have always operated' with no ATO is a critical finding.
probes: Has the AO formally accepted any residual risks? Show me the acceptance language.
Is this a traditional ATO or an ongoing authorization under continuous monitoring?

questions.question: When was the last risk assessment performed for this system, and how did its results influence control selection, tailoring, or remediation priorities?
questions.whyItMatters: Risk assessment is the connective tissue between categorization and the controls actually chosen. If it is stale or ignored, the control set may not address the system's real threats.
evidence: Risk assessment report (per NIST SP 800-30 or equivalent)
Risk register entries for the system
questions.guidance: Look for a documented methodology, identified threats and vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact analysis, and a demonstrable line from assessment results to control decisions or POA&M items.
probes: What were the top three risks identified, and what did you do about each?
How often is the risk assessment refreshed?

questions.question: Does the organization maintain an organization-wide information security program plan, and how does this system's security activity plug into that program?
questions.whyItMatters: PM-family controls are organization-level. If there is no security program plan, system-level controls are ad hoc and typically cannot be sustained between audits.
evidence: Security organization chart and role descriptions
questions.guidance: A good answer shows a current program plan with defined roles (CISO, ISSOs, system owners), resources, and coordination mechanisms — and the interviewee can explain how system-level ISSO work reports up to the program.
probes: Who is accountable for the program, and to whom do they report?
How are organization-wide security requirements pushed down to individual systems?

questions.controlRef: PM-11 Mission and Business Process Definition
questions.question: How are the mission and business processes this system supports defined, and how did that definition shape the system's security and privacy requirements?
questions.whyItMatters: Controls protect the mission, not the technology. If the business processes and their dependencies aren't defined, impact levels and availability requirements are guesswork.
evidence: Business impact analysis or mission dependency mapping
questions.guidance: Expect a clear statement of the business processes the system enables, the information flows involved, and a traceable link from mission needs to availability and integrity requirements in the categorization.
probes: What happens to the mission if this system is down for 24 hours? A week?
Were mission owners consulted during categorization?

questions.question: Show me the system component inventory. How do you know it is complete and current, and how does it define what is inside the authorization boundary?
questions.whyItMatters: You cannot protect or assess what you don't know you have. Inventory gaps are the root cause of unmanaged assets, unscanned hosts, and out-of-scope findings that later become incidents.
evidence: Reconciliation records between inventory and network scans
questions.guidance: A strong answer describes automated discovery reconciled against the documented inventory, owner and location recorded per component, and a defined update frequency. A manually maintained spreadsheet last touched a year ago is a red flag.
probes: When did you last reconcile the inventory against actual network scan results?
How do new components get added to the inventory — is it part of provisioning?

questions.question: Describe the organization's overall authorization process. How many systems hold authorizations, how are authorization decisions tracked, and what happens when an ATO expires?
questions.whyItMatters: A defined, consistently applied authorization process is what makes individual ATOs meaningful. Without it, authorization decisions are inconsistent and expired ATOs quietly become unauthorized operations.
questions.guidance: Expect an inventory of authorized systems with ATO dates and expirations, a defined renewal or ongoing-authorization path, and a clear rule (ideally enforced) that systems do not operate on expired authorizations.
probes: Have any systems operated past ATO expiration in the last two years? What happened?
Who tracks upcoming ATO expirations?

phases.name: Phase 2 — Management & Governance Control Families
phases.objective: Test the design and operating effectiveness of the management-oriented families — access control, awareness and training, audit and accountability, assessment, configuration management, contingency planning, incident response, planning, program management, personnel security, risk assessment, system acquisition, and related SI/SC governance controls.

questions.question: Walk me through the full lifecycle of a user account on this system — from request and approval, through creation, periodic review, to deactivation. Who approves access, and how often are accounts recertified?
questions.whyItMatters: Unmanaged accounts — orphaned, shared, or never reviewed — are among the most common paths to unauthorized access. A broken account lifecycle undermines nearly every other access control.
evidence: List of active accounts vs. current HR roster
questions.guidance: Expect documented approval before account creation, role-based provisioning, defined review frequency (e.g., quarterly/annually), timely deactivation on termination or transfer, and evidence recertifications actually happen and result in removals.
probes: Show me an account disabled in the last quarter because of a review.
How quickly are accounts disabled after termination — show me the last three examples with timestamps.

questions.question: Which duties has the organization determined must be separated on this system, and how is that separation enforced in practice — for example, between developers, approvers, and production administrators?
questions.whyItMatters: Without separation of duties, a single person can both execute and conceal fraud or errors. This is a classic audit finding when one admin can write code, approve it, and deploy it to production.
evidence: Documented risk acceptance for any SoD conflicts
questions.guidance: A good answer names specific incompatible duty pairs, shows enforcement through role design rather than policy alone, and acknowledges any residual conflicts (small teams) with documented compensating controls and risk acceptance.
probes: Can the same person approve and execute a payment/change/deployment? Show me.
What compensating controls exist where headcount forces combined roles?

questions.question: How is least privilege implemented on this system? How are privileged accounts identified, how is administrative access granted and reviewed, and do administrators use separate accounts for admin and non-admin work?
questions.whyItMatters: Excessive privilege multiplies the damage of any compromise or mistake. Shared or always-on admin access is one of the highest-impact weaknesses an audit can find.
evidence: Screenshots of separate admin/user account configuration
questions.guidance: Expect an inventory of privileged users, periodic access reviews with evidence, separate credentials for administrative duties, and mechanisms (sudo, PAM, just-in-time elevation) rather than standing blanket admin rights.
probes: Pull the current list of users with administrator rights — who reviews it and when?
Are there any shared admin accounts? How is their use attributable to an individual?

questions.question: Describe the security and privacy awareness training program. What content do all users receive, how often, and how do you track and enforce completion?
questions.whyItMatters: Untrained users defeat technical controls. Auditors look for evidence training is delivered, current, tracked to completion, and enforced — not just that a slide deck exists.
questions.guidance: A strong answer includes annual mandatory training with completion rates near 100%, onboarding training before system access, content refreshed for current threats, and a real enforcement mechanism for non-completion.
probes: What percentage completed training this cycle — show the report.
What happens to a user who never completes training?

questions.question: What role-based security training do privileged users — system administrators, developers, incident responders — receive beyond the general awareness program?
questions.whyItMatters: Privileged users hold the keys to the system; generic awareness training does not prepare them for role-specific risks like secure administration, secure coding, or forensic evidence handling.
questions.guidance: Expect defined per-role training requirements, records showing privileged staff completed them (e.g., admin hardening, secure development, incident handling), and refresher cadence tied to role changes.
probes: Show me the training record for the most recently appointed system administrator.
What secure development training do your developers receive?

questions.question: Which events does this system log, and how was that list determined? How do you verify that logging is actually enabled on every in-scope component?
questions.whyItMatters: If the wrong events are logged — or logging silently stops on some hosts — incident detection and forensic investigation become impossible, and AU-6 review has nothing to work with.
evidence: SIEM/log source onboarding list vs. component inventory
questions.guidance: A good answer ties the logged-event list to organizational requirements and risk, covers authentication, privilege use, and security-relevant changes, and includes periodic verification that all in-scope components are actually sending logs.
probes: Show me the last time a host stopped sending logs — how was that detected?
Are failed and successful logons logged everywhere, including databases?

questions.controlRef: AU-6 Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting
questions.question: Who reviews audit logs, how often, and what are they looking for? Show me evidence that reviews happen and that anomalies found in logs have led to action.
questions.whyItMatters: Logs that nobody reviews provide zero detective value. This control is where log collection either becomes real security monitoring or wasted disk space.
evidence: Sample review notes or tickets generated from log findings
questions.guidance: Expect defined review frequency matched to risk, correlation/alerting for high-priority events, documented findings, and at least one concrete example where log review triggered an investigation or change.
probes: What was the most recent finding from log review, and what did you do?
Which events are alerted in real time versus reviewed periodically?

questions.question: How are audit logs protected from unauthorized modification or deletion — including by system administrators themselves?
questions.whyItMatters: An attacker (or insider) who can alter logs can erase evidence of their activity. Admin access to the systems that store security logs is a classic conflict auditors must probe.
questions.guidance: Look for centralized log collection outside the control of the administrators of the systems being logged, restricted access to log stores, integrity protections (WORM, immutability, signing), and retention meeting defined requirements.
probes: Can a system administrator delete their own activity logs? Demonstrate why not.
How long are logs retained, and who set that period?

questions.question: When was the last independent assessment of this system's controls, who performed it, and how were the results used?
questions.whyItMatters: Self-attestation without independent assessment is how control gaps persist for years. Assessments are also the evidentiary basis for authorization and continuous monitoring decisions.
questions.guidance: A strong answer cites an assessment within the organization's defined frequency, performed by assessors with appropriate independence, producing documented findings that fed the POA&M and authorization decision.
probes: Were all baseline controls assessed, or a sample? Who chose the sample?
What were the highest-risk findings from the last assessment?

questions.question: What are the approved baseline configurations for the system's operating systems, databases, and network devices, and how do you verify deployed systems actually match those baselines?
questions.whyItMatters: Configuration drift from hardened baselines is one of the most exploited weaknesses. A documented baseline with no compliance checking is indistinguishable from no baseline at all.
evidence: Hardening standards (e.g., CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs)
questions.guidance: Expect named, versioned baselines (CIS/STIG or vendor equivalent), automated compliance scanning with pass rates, documented and approved deviations, and baselines updated when platforms change.
probes: What percentage of systems currently pass the baseline scan? Show the report.
Show me a documented deviation and its approval.

questions.question: How are changes to the system analyzed for security impact before implementation, and who signs off that a change will not degrade security controls?
questions.whyItMatters: Unassessed changes silently break controls — opening ports, disabling logging, weakening authentication. Security impact analysis is what connects change management to the authorization.
evidence: Change tickets with security impact analysis section
Examples of changes rejected or modified for security reasons
questions.guidance: A good answer shows security impact analysis embedded in the change workflow, ISSO/security review participation, and a trigger for SSP or significant-change evaluation when changes affect the security posture.
probes: Show me three recent change tickets and their security impact analysis.
What defines a 'significant change' that requires authorization review?

questions.question: Show me the contingency plan for this system. Does it define recovery objectives, roles, and procedures for restoring the system after disruption, and is it consistent with the availability impact level?
questions.whyItMatters: A system categorized moderate or high for availability must have recovery capabilities to match. A plan that doesn't reflect the actual system — or doesn't exist — leaves the mission exposed to any disruption.
evidence: Alternate processing/storage site agreements if applicable
questions.guidance: Expect a current plan tied to the system's categorization, explicit RTO/RPO, named recovery roles and contact lists, recovery procedures specific to this system, and evidence of periodic review.
probes: What is the RTO for this system, and have you ever actually met it in a test?
Where are plan copies stored so they are available during a disaster?

questions.question: When was the contingency plan last tested, what type of test was performed, and what did you learn and change as a result?
questions.whyItMatters: Untested recovery plans fail when needed. The difference between a tabletop exercise and an actual functional recovery test tells the auditor how much confidence the RTO claims deserve.
questions.guidance: Expect tests at the organization-defined frequency with documented results, identified deficiencies, and tracked corrective actions. A functional recovery test carries far more weight than a paper walkthrough for higher-impact systems.
probes: Was the last test a tabletop, or did you actually restore systems? Show the recovery time achieved.
What corrective actions came out of the last test, and are they closed?

questions.question: Walk me through what happens when a security incident is detected on this system — from triage through containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned. Show me records from recent incidents.
questions.whyItMatters: Incident handling is where security operations prove themselves. An inability to produce records of real incident handling suggests incidents are either not being detected or not being managed.
questions.guidance: A strong answer follows a defined lifecycle, shows documented handling of real incidents with timestamps and outcomes, includes escalation criteria to the CISO/organization level, and closes with lessons learned feeding control improvements.
probes: Show me the most significant incident from the past year and how it was handled end to end.
What changed after that incident?

questions.question: What are the requirements and timelines for reporting incidents — internally and to external bodies (e.g., US-CERT/CISA, agency SOC, or contractual reporting) — and how do you verify reporting actually happens within those timelines?
questions.whyItMatters: Late or missed external reporting can violate law, regulation, or contract and prevents coordinated response. Auditors need evidence the timelines are known and met.
questions.guidance: Expect explicit reporting timelines (e.g., federal one-hour reporting to CISA where applicable), a defined channel and responsible role, and records demonstrating past reports met the deadline — or an honest statement there were no reportable incidents with evidence detection is working.
probes: What is your external reporting deadline and to whom?
Show me the last incident reported externally and when it was sent relative to detection.

questions.question: How and when is the incident response capability tested, and do the people who would actually respond participate?
questions.whyItMatters: Untested response plans fail under stress. Tabletop participation by the real responders — not just the security team — reveals coordination gaps before a real incident does.
questions.guidance: Look for tests at least annually (or organization-defined), scenarios realistic for this system's threats, participation across IT ops, management, and communications roles, and documented improvements afterward.
probes: When was the last exercise, and who sat at the table?
What was the top lesson from the last exercise, and was it fixed?

questions.question: Show me the incident response plan. Does it cover this system specifically, and when was it last updated based on incidents or tests?
questions.whyItMatters: A generic template plan that doesn't name this system's contacts, data types, and procedures will not hold up in a real incident. Currency is the proxy for whether the plan is alive.
questions.guidance: Expect a plan tailored to the system or organization, updated within the last year or after incidents/tests, with current contact information, defined reportable incident types, and metrics or lessons-learned integration.
probes: When was the contact list last verified? Call out one change made after the last incident.
Does the plan address privacy breach response, not just security incidents?

questions.question: What background screening is required before individuals are granted access to this system, and is rescreening performed? Show evidence screening is completed before access is granted.
questions.whyItMatters: Insider risk cannot be managed if people are granted access before vetting completes. Auditors check that screening precedes access — not that paperwork eventually catches up.
evidence: Sample of completed screening records matched to access grant dates
questions.guidance: A good answer ties screening level to position risk designation, shows screening completed before access in sampled cases, and includes rescreening or continuous evaluation for sensitive roles where required.
probes: Pick three users granted access this year — show screening completion dates versus access dates.
Are contractors screened to the same standard?

questions.question: Walk me through what happens, hour by hour, when someone with access to this system is terminated or resigns. How quickly is access revoked, and how do you verify it?
questions.whyItMatters: Terminated employees retaining access is a top insider-threat vector. The termination workflow is auditable end to end — tickets, timestamps, and property return either exist or they don't.
evidence: Recent termination tickets with access-revocation timestamps
questions.guidance: Expect HR-to-IT notification within hours, deactivation within the organization-defined period (often same day), retrieval of badges and equipment, and a sample demonstrating actual timestamps meet the requirement — including for involuntary terminations.
probes: Show me the last three terminations and when each account was disabled.
What happens differently for an involuntary termination?

questions.question: What happens to access rights when an employee transfers to a different role or department? How do you prevent privilege accumulation over time?
questions.whyItMatters: Privilege accumulation — 'access creep' — means long-tenured staff often hold far more access than their job requires. Transfers are where least privilege quietly erodes.
evidence: Examples of access removed on transfer
questions.guidance: A strong answer includes a transfer-triggered review that removes old-role access before or as new access is granted, plus periodic recertification to catch anything missed.
probes: Show me a recent transfer and which old permissions were removed.
Is removal of old access automatic or dependent on someone remembering?

questions.question: How are vulnerability scans performed on this system — scope, frequency, tooling — and how do scan results flow into remediation with defined timelines by severity?
questions.whyItMatters: Scanning without remediation timelines is theater. Auditors test whether high/critical findings are actually patched within policy windows and whether scan scope covers the whole boundary.
evidence: Tickets showing remediation of critical findings
questions.guidance: Expect authenticated scans covering the full inventory at defined frequency, severity-based remediation deadlines (e.g., critical 15/30 days), evidence of meeting them, and exceptions documented and risk-accepted.
probes: Show me current unremediated critical findings older than your SLA.
Are scans credentialed/authenticated? Why or why not?

questions.question: How are security and privacy requirements embedded into contracts and acquisition documents for the products and services used by this system?
questions.whyItMatters: If security requirements aren't in the contract, they cannot be enforced on vendors. This is the front door for supply chain and outsourced-service risk.
evidence: Recent contract with security requirements section
questions.guidance: Look for standard security requirement language (controls, incident notification, right to audit, data handling) applied consistently, and evidence security staff review acquisitions before signature.
probes: Show me the security section of a contract signed this year.
Who reviews security requirements before a contract is executed?

questions.question: Which external services does this system depend on (cloud, SaaS, outsourced operations), and how do you verify those providers meet your security requirements — for example through FedRAMP, SOC 2, or contract terms?
questions.whyItMatters: Outsourcing a service does not outsource the risk. The organization remains responsible for verifying provider controls, and the SSP must accurately describe what is inherited versus self-implemented.
questions.guidance: A strong answer enumerates external services, shows current independent attestations reviewed by security staff, and documents which controls are inherited from providers versus implemented internally.
probes: For your cloud provider, which controls do you inherit and which remain yours?
When did you last review the provider's SOC 2 or FedRAMP package?

questions.question: What security testing do developers perform before code is deployed to production — static/dynamic analysis, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing — and what happens when testing finds flaws?
questions.whyItMatters: Application-level flaws introduced by development bypass infrastructure controls. Evidence of pre-deployment security testing and a fix-or-accept workflow is the difference between secure SDLC and hopeful coding.
evidence: SAST/DAST scan reports for recent releases
questions.guidance: Expect defined pre-deployment security testing gates, results retained per release, severity-based remediation before deployment, and documented risk acceptance for anything deployed with known flaws.
probes: Show me the security test results for the last production release.
Has any release shipped with known critical flaws? Who accepted that risk?

questions.question: How are software flaws identified, prioritized, and remediated on this system? What are the patch timelines by severity, and what is the current patch compliance rate?
questions.whyItMatters: Unpatched known vulnerabilities are the most common root cause of breaches. The audit question is not whether patches exist but whether remediation happens within defined, risk-based timeframes.
evidence: Examples of emergency patching for critical CVEs
questions.guidance: Look for defined remediation windows tied to severity, measured compliance against those windows, a process for emergency patches, and documented handling of systems that cannot be patched (compensating controls, risk acceptance).
probes: What percentage of systems are within patch SLA right now?
Show me how you handled the last critical, widely exploited vulnerability.

phases.name: Phase 3 — Operational & Technical Control Families Walkthrough
phases.objective: Walk through the operational and technical families — identification and authentication, maintenance, media protection, physical and environmental protection, PII processing and transparency, system and communications protection, system and information integrity technical controls, and the Rev. 5 supply chain family — verifying controls work in practice, not just on paper.

questions.question: How are users uniquely identified and authenticated to this system, and where is multifactor authentication enforced — including for remote access and privileged accounts?
questions.whyItMatters: Single-factor authentication on remote or privileged access is among the highest-risk findings in any audit. Unique identification is also the prerequisite for accountability in audit logs.
evidence: List of accounts exempt from MFA with justification
questions.guidance: Expect MFA enforced for remote access and privileged users (at minimum), unique accounts per person with no shared user credentials, and any MFA exceptions documented, time-limited, and risk-accepted.
probes: Show me an account that authenticates with password only — why does it exist?
Is MFA phishing-resistant (e.g., PIV/FIDO2), and for whom?

questions.question: How are passwords and other authenticators managed — complexity or length requirements, secure storage, handling of default and service account credentials?
questions.whyItMatters: Weak authenticator management (default passwords, plaintext storage, unmanaged service accounts) routinely defeats otherwise strong identification controls.
evidence: Service account inventory with credential rotation records
questions.guidance: A good answer shows enforced authenticator standards aligned to NIST SP 800-63B (length over forced complexity), salted/hashed credential storage, service account credentials vaulted and rotated, and verification that vendor default passwords were changed.
probes: How are service account passwords managed and rotated?
When did you last verify no default credentials remain on network devices?

questions.question: How is remote/nonlocal maintenance performed on this system — who is allowed, through what path, with what authentication, and how are sessions monitored and logged?
questions.whyItMatters: Vendor and administrator remote maintenance channels are prime attack paths. Unmonitored vendor access has been the entry point in major public breaches.
evidence: Session logs or recordings of remote maintenance
questions.guidance: Expect remote maintenance only through approved, MFA-protected paths, per-session or time-bound vendor authorization, session monitoring/logging, and termination of sessions when work completes.
probes: Show me the last vendor maintenance session and its approval.
Do vendors have standing access, or is it enabled per session?

questions.question: How do you obtain maintenance support and spare parts within the timeframes needed to meet this system's availability requirements?
questions.whyItMatters: A high-availability categorization is meaningless if a failed component takes weeks to replace. Timely maintenance links the contingency plan's RTO to real support contracts.
questions.guidance: Expect support agreements with response times consistent with the system's availability impact level and RTO, evidence SLAs are met, and spares for critical single points of failure.
probes: Which single component failure would take longest to recover from, and why?
When did a support SLA last get exercised, and was it met?

questions.question: How is access to digital and non-digital media containing this system's data restricted — backups, removable drives, printed output?
questions.whyItMatters: Media that anyone can pick up bypasses every logical access control. Backup tapes and printed reports are routinely overlooked in otherwise well-controlled environments.
questions.guidance: Look for media stored in controlled areas, access restricted to authorized personnel, removable media use restricted and approved, and printed sensitive output handled per policy.
probes: Where are backups stored, and who can physically reach them?
Is USB/removable media allowed? How is it controlled?

questions.question: How is media sanitized before disposal or reuse — what methods are used for different media types, and what records prove sanitization happened?
questions.whyItMatters: Improperly sanitized drives and devices are a recurring source of data exposure. Certificates of destruction and sanitization logs are the evidence this control is real.
questions.guidance: Expect techniques matched to media type and data sensitivity (clear, purge, destroy per 800-88), tracked per device with certificates or logs, and verification sampling of sanitized media.
probes: Show me destruction certificates from the last equipment refresh.
How are failed drives under warranty handled — are they ever returned unsanitized?

questions.question: Who is authorized for physical access to the facilities housing this system, how is that list maintained, and how quickly is access removed when roles change or people leave?
questions.whyItMatters: Physical access defeats logical access. Stale badge lists with former employees still authorized are a common and serious finding.
evidence: Access removal records tied to terminations/transfers
questions.guidance: Expect a maintained authorization list reviewed periodically, badge access deactivated promptly on termination or transfer, and physical access aligned to job need rather than convenience.
probes: Reconcile the badge list against current staff — any names that shouldn't be there?
How quickly are badges deactivated after termination?

questions.question: Walk me through the physical controls protecting the server rooms and equipment — entry control, visitor handling, and how physical access is logged and reviewed.
questions.whyItMatters: Tailgating, unescorted visitors, and unlogged entry are the physical equivalents of shared accounts. Auditors verify controls at the door, not just in the policy.
evidence: Photos or walkthrough of server room entry controls
Review records of physical access logs
questions.guidance: A good walkthrough shows controlled entry points (badge/biometric), visitor escort and logging, retention and periodic review of physical access logs, and alarms or guards appropriate to the impact level.
probes: Show me the physical access log review — who reviews it and how often?
How are visitors and vendors escorted in the data center?

questions.question: How is physical access to the system monitored — cameras, intrusion alarms, review of badge logs — and how would you detect someone entering outside authorized patterns?
questions.whyItMatters: Physical entry without monitoring is undetected access. For moderate/high impact systems, detection capability is expected, not just locked doors.
evidence: Camera coverage map and retention settings
Intrusion alarm configuration and test records
questions.guidance: Expect monitored entry points, functioning alarms with test evidence, camera retention sufficient for investigation, and correlation of physical logs with incidents when needed.
probes: How long is camera footage retained?
When was the intrusion detection system last tested?

questions.question: If this system processes personally identifiable information, what is the documented authority and purpose for processing it, and how is that purpose enforced in the system's design?
questions.whyItMatters: Rev. 5 added the PT family because privacy failures now carry legal and mission risk equal to security failures. Processing PII without documented authority exposes the organization regardless of how good security controls are.
questions.guidance: Expect a clear statement of legal/mission authority for PII processing, a completed PIA or equivalent analysis, defined processing purposes, and design decisions (minimization, retention limits) consistent with that purpose.
probes: Which PII elements does the system collect, and which could be eliminated without harming the mission?
Who is accountable for privacy compliance for this system?

questions.question: How do you ensure PII is actually used only for the documented purposes — and how would you detect or prevent function creep into new uses?
questions.whyItMatters: Function creep — repurposing collected PII for new uses without review — is the most common real-world privacy failure. Purpose limitation must be operational, not aspirational.
evidence: Data use policies and access rules by purpose
Change/approval records for new uses of PII
Privacy review of new features using PII
questions.guidance: A strong answer shows new uses of PII require review/approval before implementation, access is scoped to purpose, and periodic checks confirm actual use matches documented purposes.
probes: Has the system's use of PII changed since the PIA? Was the PIA updated?
Who approves a new report or feature that touches PII?

questions.question: Describe the boundary protections for this system — firewalls, segmentation, DMZs, managed interfaces — and how firewall rules are reviewed and recertified.
questions.whyItMatters: Flat networks and stale firewall rules allow a compromise anywhere to reach the system. Rule-base review evidence is where theoretical segmentation is proven or disproven.
evidence: Firewall rule sets with last review date
questions.guidance: Expect documented boundary architecture, deny-by-default posture, business justification per rule, periodic rule recertification with removals, and segmentation between the system and general user/corporate networks.
probes: When was the firewall rule base last recertified, and how many rules were removed?
Can the general user network reach the database tier directly? Demonstrate.

questions.question: How is data in transit protected — which protocols and cipher suites are permitted, and how do you verify no weak or deprecated encryption remains in service?
questions.whyItMatters: Deprecated TLS versions and unencrypted internal traffic expose data to interception. Auditors check configuration evidence, not policy statements.
evidence: Protocol/cipher configuration exports from load balancers and services
questions.guidance: Expect approved cryptographic standards (e.g., TLS 1.2+ with approved ciphers), scans showing deprecated protocols disabled, encryption for external and sensitive internal flows, and certificates managed with expiry monitoring.
probes: Show me scan results proving TLS 1.0/1.1 are disabled.
Is internal traffic between application tiers encrypted?

questions.controlRef: SC-12 Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management
questions.question: How are cryptographic keys generated, stored, rotated, and destroyed for this system? Who can access key material?
questions.whyItMatters: Encryption with unmanaged keys is a false sense of security — hardcoded keys in source code and keys stored next to the data they protect are recurring audit findings.
questions.guidance: Look for documented key lifecycle, keys stored in KMS/HSM or protected vaults rather than config files, defined rotation, restricted access, and no secrets in source repositories (verified by scanning).
probes: Where do application secrets live — show me how a deployed app retrieves its database password.
When were production keys last rotated?

questions.controlRef: SC-28 Protection of Information at Rest
questions.question: What data at rest is encrypted on this system — databases, file stores, backups, endpoints — and how was that scope decided?
questions.whyItMatters: Unencrypted backups and databases turn any theft or misplacement into a breach. The scope decision must trace back to the confidentiality impact level.
evidence: Data classification mapping to encryption requirements
questions.guidance: Expect encryption for data stores consistent with the confidentiality categorization — including backups and replicas — with keys managed per SC-12, and any unencrypted stores documented and justified.
probes: Are backups encrypted? Show the setting.
Which data stores are not encrypted, and who accepted that?

questions.question: How is malicious code protection deployed across the system — what tools, on which platforms, and how do you know signatures/engines are current everywhere?
questions.whyItMatters: Anti-malware with stale definitions or coverage gaps (servers and Linux hosts are commonly missed) provides little real protection. Central reporting is the proof of currency.
questions.guidance: A good answer shows centralized management with a coverage report reconciled to the component inventory, automatic updates verified current, detections investigated, and protection on workstations, servers, and email/web gateways.
probes: Show me hosts where the agent is not reporting — how many and why?
Show me the most recent real detection and how it was handled.

questions.question: How is the system monitored for attacks and indicators of compromise — what monitoring tools and use cases are deployed, where, and who watches the output around the clock or responds to alerts?
questions.whyItMatters: SI-4 is the core detective control of the baseline. Monitoring deployed but unwatched, or covering only the perimeter while east-west traffic goes unobserved, leaves the organization blind to active compromise.
evidence: Alert triage tickets with response times
questions.guidance: Expect monitoring across perimeter, internal network, and endpoints; documented detection use cases tied to threats; defined alert triage with measured response times; and evidence alerts lead to investigation (link to IR-4 records).
probes: Who is alerted at 2 a.m. on a Saturday, and what do they do?
Show me a recent alert escalated to an incident.
Is internal/east-west traffic monitored, or only the perimeter?

questions.controlRef: SI-7 Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity
questions.question: How do you verify the integrity of software, firmware, and critical system files — integrity checking tools, allowlisting, secure boot — and how are integrity violations handled?
questions.whyItMatters: Integrity verification is how unauthorized changes and sophisticated malware (rootkits, tampered binaries) are detected. Its absence is especially significant on high-impact systems.
evidence: File integrity monitoring configuration and reports
Application allowlisting policy and enforcement evidence
questions.guidance: Expect file integrity monitoring on critical system files with alerts investigated, allowlisting where defined by the baseline or tailoring, and integrity checks incorporated into change and incident workflows.
probes: Show me the last integrity alert and its disposition.
Is application allowlisting in enforcement mode or audit mode? Why?

questions.controlRef: SR-3 Supply Chain Controls and Processes
questions.question: What supply chain controls and processes protect the acquisition of the hardware, software, and services this system depends on — from vetting suppliers through delivery and integration?
questions.whyItMatters: The SR family is new in Rev. 5 in response to real supply chain compromises (e.g., tampered software updates). Organizations that have not operationalized SR-3 lack defenses against compromised or counterfeit components.
evidence: Software bills of materials (SBOMs) where used
questions.guidance: A good answer describes a documented SCRM process: approved supplier lists, integrity/authenticity verification of software and updates, SBOM or component analysis for critical software, and contractual flow-down of security requirements.
probes: How do you verify a software update is authentic before deploying it?
Which suppliers are considered critical, and how were they vetted?

questions.question: How are critical suppliers assessed and periodically reviewed for security risk — what assessments, attestations, or audits do you require, and what happens when a supplier fails review?
questions.whyItMatters: One-time onboarding vetting goes stale. Supplier assessments and reviews are how the organization catches deteriorating supplier security before it becomes the organization's incident.
evidence: Third-party attestation review records (SOC 2, ISO certs)
Remediation or exit records for failed suppliers
questions.guidance: Expect tiered assessment rigor by supplier criticality, periodic re-assessment, review of independent attestations, and at least one example (or a defined process) for handling suppliers that fail review.
probes: When were your three most critical suppliers last reassessed?
Have you ever exited or remediated a supplier relationship for security reasons?

questions.question: Do agreements with critical suppliers require them to notify you of security incidents, compromises, or supply chain disruptions affecting the products or services you depend on — and has that ever been exercised?
questions.whyItMatters: Without contractual notification, the organization may learn of a supplier compromise from the news. Notification clauses convert supply chain risk into actionable incident response time.
evidence: Records of supplier notifications received and handled
questions.guidance: Look for explicit notification requirements with timeframes in contracts with critical suppliers, a defined internal path to handle such notifications, and any real examples of receiving and acting on one.
probes: Show me the notification clause in a critical supplier contract.
What would you do if a key software vendor announced their build system was compromised?

questions.controlRef: SC-20 / SC-21 Secure Name Resolution & Recursive Resolution
questions.question: How is name resolution secured for this system — are DNS services authenticated and integrity-protected, and do internal resolvers use trusted, protected resolution paths?
questions.whyItMatters: DNS manipulation silently redirects users and systems to attacker infrastructure. Secure name resolution is a small control with outsized impact on data-in-transit trust.
evidence: Resolver configuration (validated resolvers, DNSSEC where applicable)
questions.guidance: Expect use of authenticated/trusted resolvers, protective DNS filtering for outbound queries, and DNSSEC validation or signing where applicable — with configuration evidence rather than assertions.
probes: Which resolvers do endpoints and servers use, and who controls them?
Is DNS query filtering in place, and what has it blocked recently?

phases.name: Phase 4 — Continuous Monitoring & Assessment (CA-7)
phases.objective: Evaluate the continuous monitoring strategy: whether it defines metrics and assessment frequencies per control, whether monitoring results are current and actually consumed by decision-makers, and whether the authorization is maintained through ongoing awareness rather than point-in-time paperwork.

questions.question: Describe the continuous monitoring strategy for this system. Which controls are monitored at what frequency, what metrics are collected, and who approved the strategy?
questions.whyItMatters: Continuous monitoring is the Rev. 5 mechanism that keeps an authorization honest between assessments. A strategy that exists only as a document, with no defined metrics or frequencies, means the ATO's assumptions decay invisibly.
evidence: Authorizing Official approval of the strategy
questions.guidance: A strong answer presents an approved strategy defining which controls are monitored continuously versus periodically, organization-defined frequencies matched to risk, and explicit ties to the authorization decision (ongoing authorization or reauthorization triggers).
probes: Which controls do you monitor monthly, quarterly, and annually — show the matrix.
Did the Authorizing Official approve this strategy? Show me.

questions.question: Show me the actual security status reporting produced by continuous monitoring — recent dashboards, metrics, or status reports — and who receives and acts on them.
questions.whyItMatters: Monitoring that produces reports nobody reads is indistinguishable from no monitoring. The auditor needs evidence the output reaches decision-makers and changes behavior.
evidence: Recent monthly/quarterly security status reports or dashboards
Distribution lists and meeting minutes where reports are reviewed
Decisions or actions traceable to a status report
questions.guidance: Expect current, dated status reporting (not a template), delivered to the System Owner and Authorizing Official on the defined cadence, and at least one concrete decision or POA&M change traceable to the reporting.
probes: Show me the last three status reports — what changed between them?
Tell me about a decision made because of a monitoring report.

questions.question: Does continuous monitoring include independent assessment of controls on an ongoing basis, rather than relying solely on the system team's self-monitoring?
questions.whyItMatters: Self-monitoring alone lets drift and bias persist. Independent assessment within the conmon program is what gives the Authorizing Official confidence the reported status reflects reality.
evidence: Assessment reports produced under the conmon program
questions.guidance: For moderate/high systems, expect a rolling independent assessment of control subsets each year with reports feeding the authorization, plus clear separation between those who operate controls and those who assess them.
probes: Which controls were independently assessed in the last 12 months?
How do assessment findings from independent assessors differ from the team's self-reported status?

questions.question: How do vulnerability scanning results feed continuous monitoring — are scan trends reported over time, and are recurring or aging findings escalated?
questions.whyItMatters: Vulnerability trend data is one of the most objective conmon inputs. Flat or worsening trends that nobody escalates indicate the monitoring loop is broken.
evidence: Integration of scan data into status dashboards
questions.guidance: Look for trending (not just point-in-time) vulnerability data included in conmon reporting, automatic escalation of findings past SLA, and visible improvement or explained variance over time.
probes: What is the trend in critical findings over the past year?
What is the oldest open critical finding right now, and why is it still open?

questions.question: How does configuration compliance monitoring run on an ongoing basis — are configuration settings continuously checked against the approved baselines, and how is drift detected and corrected?
questions.whyItMatters: Baselines verified once a year are wrong most of the year. Continuous configuration compliance checking is the difference between a hardened environment and a hardened moment.
evidence: Continuous configuration compliance scan schedule and results
questions.guidance: Expect automated, recurring compliance checking against CM-2 baselines with current compliance rates, alerts or tickets for drift, and remediation tracked to closure — plus reporting of drift metrics into conmon status.
probes: How quickly after a baseline deviation would you know about it?
Show me a drift detection from this quarter and its resolution.

questions.question: How does the organization-wide program monitor the effectiveness of security controls across systems — and how does this system's monitoring roll up into that program view?
questions.whyItMatters: PM-14 is the organizational counterpart to CA-7. Without a program-level view, systemic weaknesses recur across systems and leadership cannot see aggregate risk.
evidence: Leadership review minutes (e.g., risk executive function)
questions.guidance: A good answer shows aggregated metrics across systems (assessment results, POA&M aging, incident trends), regular review by senior leadership or a risk executive function, and system-level reporting that demonstrably feeds it.
probes: What does the CISO/dashboard show about this system right now?
What organization-wide control weakness did the program identify recently, and what changed?

questions.question: How does continuous monitoring affect the authorization itself — is this system under ongoing authorization, and what events would trigger reauthorization or a change to the authorization decision?
questions.whyItMatters: Ongoing authorization only works if significant-change and risk-threshold triggers are defined and enforced. Otherwise 'continuous' authorization quietly becomes permanent authorization.
evidence: Significant change definition and trigger list
Records of reauthorization or authorization updates
questions.guidance: Expect an explicit definition of significant change, documented triggers for AO re-review (major incidents, new threats, system changes), and at least one instance where monitoring results changed the authorization posture — or a defensible explanation of stable status.
probes: What would constitute a significant change requiring AO re-review?
Has the AO's risk acceptance ever been revisited because of monitoring results?

phases.name: Phase 5 — Findings & POA&M
phases.objective: Confirm that weaknesses are captured accurately in a Plan of Action & Milestones, prioritized by risk, remediated within milestones, and closed only with evidence — and that the POA&M informs authorization and continuous monitoring rather than becoming a write-only list.

questions.controlRef: CA-5 Plan of Action and Milestones
questions.question: Show me the current POA&M for this system. How does every identified weakness get onto it, and how are entries structured — milestones, resources, owners, and scheduled completion dates?
questions.whyItMatters: The POA&M is the official record of known, accepted, and planned-to-fix weaknesses. Weaknesses that never reach the POA&M are invisible to the Authorizing Official, which defeats the entire risk management framework.
evidence: Current POA&M document or tool export
Intake process showing how assessment/audit/incident findings become entries
Sample entries with milestones and owners
questions.guidance: Expect a current POA&M where every entry has a weakness description, source, risk/severity, responsible owner, milestones, resources required, and completion date. Verify the intake path by tracing a recent audit or assessment finding to a POA&M entry.
probes: Trace the last assessment's findings — is every one on the POA&M?
How many entries are past their scheduled completion date?

questions.controlRef: CA-5 Plan of Action and Milestones
questions.question: How are POA&M items prioritized and remediated — what determines the order and deadlines, and what is the process and evidence for closing an item?
questions.whyItMatters: POA&Ms that grow but never shrink are risk inventories, not remediation plans. Closure without evidence is how fixed-on-paper weaknesses return in the next assessment.
evidence: Closed items with supporting remediation evidence (tickets, configs, test results)
questions.guidance: A strong answer shows risk-based prioritization (severity, exposure, exploitation), realistic milestones with slip management, and a closure process requiring verified evidence — ideally independent confirmation — before an item is marked closed.
probes: Show me a recently closed item and the evidence that verified the fix.
What happens when a milestone slips — who approves the new date?

questions.question: When a weakness cannot be remediated on schedule, how is the residual risk reassessed and formally accepted — and by whom?
questions.whyItMatters: Open-ended risk acceptance by the wrong person, or no reassessment at all, means risk decisions are being made by default rather than by accountable officials.
evidence: Risk acceptance memos with named approver and expiry
Reassessment records for delayed POA&M items
questions.guidance: Expect risk acceptance at the appropriate level (AO or delegated authority), time-limited rather than indefinite, based on reassessed likelihood and impact, and reflected in the POA&M and authorization documentation.
probes: Show me a current risk acceptance — when does it expire and who signed it?
Has any risk acceptance ever been revoked or escalated?

questions.question: How do findings from this audit (or any assessment) get validated with the system team, rated for severity, and communicated to the Authorizing Official?
questions.whyItMatters: The finding-to-decision pipeline determines whether leadership's risk picture matches reality. Disagreements about findings must be resolved on evidence, not negotiated away.
evidence: Records of findings transmitted to the AO
questions.guidance: Expect a defined process for factual-accuracy review of findings, consistent severity criteria, documented resolution of disagreements, and evidence the AO receives unfiltered assessment results along with the POA&M.
probes: What happens when the system owner disputes a finding?
Does the AO see all findings, or a summarized subset? Who decides?

questions.controlRef: PM-4 Plan of Action and Milestones Process
questions.question: At the organization level, how are POA&Ms from all systems managed and reviewed — is there a central process or tool, and what does leadership see about aggregate weakness trends?
questions.whyItMatters: PM-4 elevates the POA&M from a system artifact to an organizational risk management tool. Without it, systemic weaknesses (e.g., patching failures across many systems) are never addressed at the root.
evidence: Organization-wide POA&M process description or tool
Aggregate POA&M metrics reported to leadership
questions.guidance: Look for a consolidated view of POA&Ms across systems, leadership reporting on volume, aging, and severity trends, and evidence that recurring cross-system weaknesses drive program-level fixes (funding, tooling, policy).
probes: What is the aggregate count and aging of open weaknesses across systems?
Give an example of a systemic weakness fixed at the program level rather than system by system.

questions.controlRef: PL-2 System Security and Privacy Plan
questions.question: After findings are remediated or the system changes, how are the SSP, risk assessment, and other authorization documents updated so they stay accurate?
questions.whyItMatters: Documentation that drifts from reality invalidates the basis of the authorization. The SSP update discipline is the final test of whether the RMF lifecycle actually loops.
evidence: SSP revision history aligned to changes and remediations
questions.guidance: Expect defined triggers (significant change, remediation completion, annual review) that update the SSP and related documents, revision history demonstrating this happens, and re-approval where the change is significant.
probes: Show me an SSP update made because of a remediation or system change.
Who verifies the SSP still matches reality, and when did that last happen?

questions.question: How do lessons learned from incidents, assessments, and audits feed back into the security program — plans, training, control implementations — with a concrete recent example?
questions.whyItMatters: Findings and incidents that produce no change guarantee repeat findings. A worked example of lessons-learned driving a concrete improvement is the strongest evidence of a functioning security program.
evidence: Training content updated after an incident or finding
questions.guidance: A good answer cites a specific recent incident or finding, the corrective action assigned, the change made (plan, control, training), and verification the change is in effect — not just a meeting where lessons were 'discussed'.
probes: What is the most recent control improvement that originated from a lesson learned?
How are corrective actions tracked to completion?
